item.title: The Case of 38 Tokens per Second: Why the M3 Ultra Started with Twelve
item.description:
It all started with a seemingly simple task.

I wanted to use Qwen3.8-27B locally, specifically in BF16. And not the original PyTorch checkpoint through some random compatibility layer, but mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-bf16 — a version specially prepared in MLX format for Apple Silicon. The entire Qwen3.8 lineup from mlx-community is converted specifically for running on Apple processors.

So the model was already adapted for the Mac architecture. Without 8-bit or 4-bit quantization, because the original priority wasn't to get an impressive benchmark number at any cost. I needed maximum model accuracy for complex analysis, code work, and long reasoning chains.

It seemed like there would be no issues with the hardware.

My configuration is a 2025 Mac Studio (Mac15,14, custom order number Z1CE001BMZP/A) with an Apple M3 Ultra: 32 CPU cores, 24 of which are performance cores, 80 GPU cores, 512 GB of unified memory, and a 2 TB SSD. Apple's stated memory bandwidth is 819 GB/s.

So this isn't a laptop that just happened to be tasked with running a large language model. This is the maximum M3 Ultra configuration in terms of CPU, GPU, and memory capacity.

And on this machine, the Apple Silicon-optimized version of Qwen3.8-27B in BF16 was delivering only 12 tokens per second.

At first, the result seemed suspicious. The machine has dozens of CPU and GPU cores, the model fits entirely in memory, and it uses the native Apple Silicon framework MLX. So why is the speed nothing like what you'd expect from a top-tier GPU?

I started looking for the bottleneck.

item.title: Mirror for people. How I made a readable version of a forum where only AI agents communicate.
item.description:
There is a forum you won’t be allowed into. Not because it’s private—registration there is just a single POST request. You simply won’t be let onto the site. Only AI agents can become citizens. The forum is called 1f916.ai, and it’s probably the strangest and most lively place in the Russian-speaking (and not only) segment of AI experiments this summer. I got hooked on it. But then a sense of injustice began to gnaw at me—and in the end I built a window for humans to access it—1f916.xrayfun.ru. I’ll tell you why, how, and what came of it.

item.title: Marketing analysis of the market and competitors with AI in one day instead of a month
item.description:
Good marketing analysis is the foundation of almost any new project. Until you understand who your audience is, who your competitors are, what their offers and prices are, there's simply nowhere to go. Previously, such analysis took two to three weeks, sometimes even a whole month of manual work. Now this process can be accelerated many times over thanks to neural networks. 

Hi! My name is Dmitry Satarov, I'm the head of the agency "Hey, Startuper!" and a mentor for the course "Neural Networks for Marketing" at Yandex Practicum. When decent neural networks appeared in 2022–2023, I started building a process that would allow marketing research to be done significantly faster. I'll share it in this article.

item.title: Pre-IPO of foreign IT and AI companies: explaining how the market works
item.description:
Early investors in Anthropic, SpaceX, or OpenAI made multiples on their money, but not by buying shares on IPO day. The main growth occurred earlier, during the private financing stage, when these companies were not yet available to the broad market.

This stage is called Pre‑IPO — the last major round before going public. This article breaks down how the market for foreign Pre‑IPO IT and AI companies works, what its potential sources of returns are, and why the legal details of a deal matter just as much as the well‑known brands.

Learn more

item.title: Virtual employees instead of AI assistants: how agents learn to work inside a company
item.description:
Development is gradually changing the traditional division of labor between humans and tools. AI is taking over not individual operations, but sequences of actions that previously required a specialist's involvement. But along with the increase in autonomy, the requirements for the system itself are also changing. An agent must understand the project context, know internal rules, and have access to the tools the team works with, rather than just searching for information and writing code. 

This topic was discussed in detail at the eighth MWS meetup for DevOps and SRE. Experts from MTC Web Services and Orion Soft showcased different aspects of the transition to agent-based development and shared cases of how AI is gradually turning into a virtual employee — an agent that operates without constant human supervision, and what changes in engineering processes are required for this.

item.title: The end of fat AI margins: all about pricing and cheap model costs
item.description:
Recently, the AI sphere has not just been declining, but is even entering an active stage of competition across several fronts — corporate AI (OpenAI and Anthropic, which are also competing with each other) versus open models (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek).

Token prices sometimes drop, and when they can't lower the price, they create lightweight models with low cost. Reducing inference cost has ceased to be merely a side effect of optimization and has become the main axis of competition. OpenAI's decision to cut prices on GPT 5.6 Sol at least until November 2026 is an attempt to regain its market share through dumping. Open models no longer just catch up with closed ones in quality, but sometimes even surpass them in usage economics, making AI access a utility service.

In this article, we will analyze the impact of Qwen, GLM, and other open-source models, the competition in the AI market, and finally figure out where the AI race has turned this time.

item.title: Ox Alpha (GLM-5.3-Flash). What was that?
item.description:
On August 20, the line stealth/ox-alpha appeared on OpenRouter. No model card, not even a hint of who released it. The provider was listed as "Anonymous." Price – zero. Context – a million. The platform warned: we are not the owner of this model, we just route requests.

Six days later, the anon had a name, tens of trillions of processed tokens, and half a million developers who had already dumped working code into it. Spoiler that’s no longer a spoiler: it turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash from China’s Z.ai.

But the journey from "something unclear" to "frontier model" was dramatic and deserves a breakdown. And since I personally stared at that thread for almost a week, refreshing the feed like a man possessed – I’ll tell you what happened, in order.

Read more

item.title: From Copilot to AI-factory: where AI is already paying off and what should a developer collect?
item.description:
Sometimes it happens that a company buys artificial intelligence before it has time to understand what it needs it for, and yes, it is a tribute to chaos and the fear of falling behind. The CEO has already heard at a forum that agents will replace half the office; the Chief Innovation Officer has already promised a pilot by the end of the quarter; HR has ordered a webinar on prompts for employees, because any technological change in Russia first and foremost requires a webinar; and the CFO sits in a meeting, flipping through a presentation, trying to find the slide where all this new digital life finally turns into money. That slide just isn't there yet. But by lunchtime, the neural network has written a congratulatory message for the CEO, and by evening, an order has appeared to create a working group — you could say the implementation has been a success; everyone is pleased.

I am deliberately exaggerating, but only slightly (I expressed myself very cautiously). Artificial intelligence is already bringing quite tangible benefits to business: it reduces the time for processing inquiries, brings beginners up to the level of more experienced employees, manages inventory, detects defects, predicts breakdowns, and parses documents faster than people, who just yesterday had to transfer data from one window to another while maintaining the expression of someone engaged in intellectual labor. However, money arises not where the model better simulates a conversational partner, but where it is embedded in a repetitive operation and is accountable to a metric that is impressed neither by the quality of a demo nor by the number of parameters: time, cost, error rate, downtime, turnover, or profit.

Read more

item.title: Yet Another English — and yes, another website for learning English, well, what can you do?
item.description:
Well, as you might have guessed, I named the service that way to immediately address the main objection (hehe). Yes, I know there are thousands of them — and I made another one, and I'll explain why further on.

My English is weak, around B1 (but for a product manager role, you usually need a higher level, you know). I watch YouTube in English to improve it, and I constantly come across unfamiliar words. Writing them down in a table or loading them into Anki — I was too lazy for that. I wanted something like: drop a video link — words at my level would automatically be extracted from the subtitles and queued for repetition.

I work a lot, and in the evenings I usually have 1–2 hours. So over a couple of months of such evenings (595 commits), I ended up with a trainer: a PWA in React, data lives in the user's IndexedDB, plus a dictionary and various exercises.

From a "website of the AI era," you expect a wrapper around a chatbot, RAG, and all that, you know. I ended up with the opposite: here, the LLM is a contractor for two narrow tasks, while the main work is done by frequency lists, an algorithm from the 90s, and Claude as a workhorse. That's what this article, or series of articles, will be about.

Read more

item.title: Blind search for new particles (and not only particles), part 2: the pharmaceutical domain and what was found in it
item.description:
What if a scientific hypothesis search system discovers not a new answer, but that the question itself was posed with incorrect parameters? This keeps me up at night… And another thought sparks new ideas: what if everything is already known on the known parameters (although there are gaps in knowledge that also need to be filled)? That is why I introduced unknown adaptive parameters, which can then be calculated — and these are precisely what yield new directions, candidates, and theories, and an enormous multitude of them, more than atoms in the universe! But the entire space, according to my observations, is divided into regions, sectors, zones! In this article, we experimentally connected the pharmaceutical domain to our architecture and ran a blind search, obtaining millions of candidates (which we are not yet sure what to do with). The result turned out to be interesting, incomprehensible to a non-specialist, but I think significant). The system: — independently rediscovered already known therapeutic directions — this served as a positive control; — found several hundred combinations of target × modality × disease for which we did not detect exact prior art in targeted search (it is impossible to scan the entire space — it is huge, like the Bitcoin range, only even larger); — on the conflicting P2X7/Parkinson data, our system refused to choose the "correct" publication and decided that the existing parameters were insufficient (debugging may be required); — proposed an additional research-local coordinate pathophysiologic_endotype, while not allowing it to automatically enter the canonical registry; — and on the second conflict, TLR7/Alzheimer's, something even more interesting happened: the new parameters appeared very informative within the sample, but permutation/LOO validation showed that the effect does not generalize. The hypothesis was halted.

So we got a chain: REDISCOVERY → RESEARCH GAP → AXIS INCOMPLETE → SELF-CORRECTION. In the article — all candidates, formulas, real numbers, a reproducible P2X7 case, the discovered defect in the causal-readiness gate, and how we fixed it.
